title: Do This, It's Good For Your Sanity
author: The Daily Stoic
summary: A short Daily Stoic entry that uses the Roman emperors as a diagnostic for modern insulation. The opening question is why so few emperors ended well, and the answer offered is less about power or wealth than about isolation: palace walls, holidays taken far from ordinary Romans, food tested for poison, and the emperor's shortcut, a concealed zigzag of ramps down to the Forum so the ruler need never touch the street. The image that carries the argument is Marcus Aurelius restricted to a private track on Palatine Hill, described as a prison yard dressed as luxury. The turn is to note that we now build the same conditions for ourselves without being forced into them, moving between house, office and car, exercising in a bubble, having food delivered, ordering everything online, meeting through screens and texting rather than calling. The prescription is correspondingly plain, that we are social animals and should be out among people, walking busy streets and running into friends. The piece ends by conceding that comfort and convenience are genuinely pleasant while insisting that too much insulation carries a cost.
points: The argument locates the emperors' undoing in isolation rather than in power or wealth, which is the less obvious of the available explanations.
The emperor's shortcut, a hidden 300-yard ramp passage to the Forum, is the concrete detail that makes the case about physical separation from ordinary life.
Marcus Aurelius on a private hilltop track is offered as luxury functioning as confinement.
The modern parallel is framed as voluntary, a list of ordinary conveniences that together remove any need to be inconvenienced or to meet anyone.
The remedy is deliberately unsophisticated, walk a busy street and be among people, on the premise that a human is a social animal.
quotes: Not many of the emperors fared well. There was something about power, something about wealth, something about temptation that, in the end, seemed to get to all of them.
Well, certainly, it’s not good for anyone to be subjected to so much pressure, such sycophancy, such abnormality and isolation. Perhaps it was the latter that weighed on them the most.
They lived behind palace walls and vacationed far away from average Romans. Their food was brought to them—tested for poison first.

Indeed, if Marcus Aurelius wanted to take a walk safely, he would have had to do it around the emperor’s private track on Palatine Hill, which, for all its luxury, was basically a prison yard for his personal use.
Meanwhile, we subject ourselves to a version of this voluntarily. We spend all our time in our house or at the office—in between, in the safe cocoon of our car.
We work remotely, take meetings through screens, text instead of call, and increasingly arrange our lives so that we rarely have to be inconvenienced or interact with anyone.
What we need to do is get outside. We need to be amongst people. We need to go for a walk on a busy city street. We need to bump into friends—and maybe meet new ones.
Comfort and convenience are nice, but too much insulation comes at a cost. We weren’t meant to experience life from inside a bubble. We were meant to be outside.
